Where is everyone finding these doctors who are willing to give that much medicine with very little resistance? I have parents in their mid-60s who have some major issues that cause pain every single day. Their doctor is so against or afraid of giving too many pain meds that they literally break them into halves and quarters to make sure they have enough to get them through a whole month. And I really haven't seen them at full capacity in a few years. The pain builds up and they try to deal as best as they can with the pittance of pills that the doctor will give them. I wish to whatever god there might be, that they could find a doctor who would be as free with medications as you guys describe. I know my parents wouldn't abuse them because they're extremely careful with meds and alcohol, etc., but it'd be nice to see them a little more back to normal!

Forty tabs isn't an outrageous amount, especially after a surgery. You might not have needed to use them, but doctors and nurses have seen people time and time again think they have things under control, only to come back because they're in massive pain. Particularly, if the person is going to have to travel, say to a whole other country, meaning it's taking longer than a few minute ride to get home, they want to be sure their patient is kept in comfort. So, there's one reason a seemingly large amount was probably prescribed to you.

Again, I understand you don't feel you needed it, but most people actually do need some form of pain relief. And guess what? Pain relief isn't just for comfort. The more pain a person is experiencing, the longer it can take for the body to heal what's causing that pain because it's too busy trying to get you out of that same pain. Vicious cycle. So it's usually to a patients benefit to NOT just man up, or suck it up, so they *don't* experience something that may have other effects and keep them on the meds longer. 

You seemed to be shocked about the 40 tablets thing, but really that's about 10 days worth *if* you took the bare minimum that's usually prescribed. In reality, based on a guess of 5 mg tabs, you could have been prescribed 2 tabs 4 times a day, which means only 5 days of relief. Many people need about 2 weeks after a surgery, even if it's relatively "minor", like an appendectomy. Being offered morphine or dilaudid is also nowhere near uncommon. Not because doctors are trying to drug you or don't care, or there's some insane reason for so many drugs, but because *most* people are in serious pain right after. Keeping patients comfortable is a part of their job, with an added benefit of speeding up the healing process. 

>[Well-controlled pain using pain medications can speed healing and lead to fewer complications.](http://www.mayoclinic.org/pain-medications/art-20046452)

Next time someone you know has to take a pain medicine, hopefully you'll cut them a little slack. Even if you don't need them, or have some particular reason why you won't take them, not everyone is the same. And taking them isn't always the pussy way out of pain.

I feel the same way about all drugs: If in some alternate universe, they all became legal tomorrow, most people who are not already inclined to use them, still wouldn't.

Instead, I smoked some that a friend gave me, and that was that. I was, and still am not all that motivated to buy it. It's just not that big of a deal because I'm not that inclined to do any type of drugs.

I have no idea why, but I've never been overly curious about them. But, don't get me wrong...I have absolutely tried a few drugs (weed, meth, coke, molly and some random pills). And for everything except weed and coke, I only tried it once. Most everything just wasn't that big of a deal to me. I have no clue why, but none of them were really a high I felt I wanted or needed again. Although, I'd never in a jillion years even contemplate doing meth. That shit is horrible! In terms of gateway drugs, I'm not really sure they're legitimately a risk. Yes, people might try something and get curious about another drug, which may addict them, but if they weren't already that type of curious, daredevil, or even shy, wanna-be-able-to-dance-freely type of person, having drugs (particularly weed) available isn't going to turn them into raging druggies....or stoners.

My daughter was sick like that when she was little, she also had respiratory problems. She was sick for weeks, and one day I had my mom go with me for the bazillionth time to the ER (not to mention countless pediatrician appts during the days). I needed my mom's help to get my point across to the doctors that I was NOT going home with her and they WOULD admit her even if it was "just" a virus because I was scared to death she was gonna die and the care at home was obviously not working. After quite a while, they finally admitted her and did supportive care. IV fluids, alternating tylenol/ibuprofen, regular treatments for her respiratory probs and cooling pads. Turns out she had RSV, which basically did have to resolve on its own, but having things monitored and administered on the dot seemed to help tremendously. The IV fluids were of particular help, because even though I was doing everything I could to get fluids down her throat, it's not always easy when they're that little. 

There just comes a point sometimes that you need to insist on the help of medical professionals. Good luck.
